concerns: Assay interference by excipients or buffer components could mimic loss of capture signal; although the design includes capture-compatibility panels and spike-in controls, these must be rigorously validated (orthogonal spike species, dose-response) to be decisive.

Upstream source-cell variability (donor, senescence, lot-to-lot differences) could confound attribution of signature loss to downstream exposures; the experiment requires >=3 independent lots from the same source-cell bank/passage range and ideally additional donor lots to bound this risk.

The linkage from an in vitro orthogonal signature loss to clinically relevant outcomes (in vivo recovery, delivery to target tissue, or potency) is unproven; Driedonks et al. highlight species- and route-dependent biodistribution limits for intranasal delivery in larger animals, so even materials that preserve the in vitro signature may fail in vivo.

Device shear simulation choices (low/mid/high) must be justified and mapped to realistic device operating regimes; otherwise the tested shear envelopes may not reflect manufacturable or clinically relevant exposures.

Relying on a qualitative pass/fail gate (yes/no loss) risks discarding materials with partial damage that could retain function; consideration of graded metrics or linking to downstream potency assays would improve decision-making.

Particle-count methods (NTA/TRPS) have limited ability to discriminate vesicular from non-vesicular particles; interpretation depends critically on orthogonal fractionation and protein:particle readouts as planned, and on maintaining sufficient material for low-biomass capture assays.
conclusion: The proposed matrixed, spike-in–controlled experiment is causally plausible and addresses an important manufacturing-quality gap: downstream stresses can plausibly disrupt membrane integrity or mask epitopes without changing bulk particle counts, producing false-positive particle-based release metrics. The plan appropriately emphasizes orthogonal intact-EV signatures (immuno-capture co-localization + detergent/protease sensitivity) and per-sample spike-in and buffer-compatibility controls to discriminate assay interference from true membrane/cargo loss. Existing community guidance and preclinical findings support the rationale but do not prove the specific downstream-exposure envelope proposed; additional controls and follow-up in vivo recoverability checks will be required before adopting a process exclusion gate.
evidence_gap: No direct experimental evidence demonstrates the specific combined envelope (freeze-thaw × device shear × low non-ionic surfactant) reproducibly abolishes the orthogonal intact-EV signature across independent lots while leaving particle counts unchanged. Key gaps include (1) spike-in–controlled matrixed in vitro data that rule out assay interference, (2) demonstration that the in vitro loss-of-signature predicts reduced in vivo recoverability or function (bridging to delivery/efficacy), and (3) validated capture-reagent compatibility across the chosen formulation/excipient panel.
